usage: to be responsible / to bear responsibility
the core pattern; 책임이 있다 means the duty rests on you
set phrase with 지다 to carry; this is how you say you will own the outcome
add -감 to mean the inner feeling of being responsible, used to describe a person
add -자 for the responsible party, e.g. the manager handling an issue
examples: 이 일은 제가 맡았으니까 끝까지 책임을 지겠습니다.
Since I took on this work, I will take responsibility for it to the end.
formal 합니다 form; common at work when committing to a task
부모는 아이에 대한 책임이 있어요.
Parents have a responsibility toward their children.
N에 대한 책임 marks who or what the responsibility is for
책임을 남에게 미루면 안 돼요.
You should not push responsibility onto others.
책임을 미루다 means to shift blame or duty away
nuance: 책임 is the abstract weight of being answerable for something, and it lives mainly through verbs: 책임을 지다 (take it on) and 책임이 있다 (it falls on you). Note that 책임 is the bare noun, while the already-common 책임감 specifically names the inner sense of duty a person feels. Use 책임 for the obligation itself and 책임감 when describing someone's character.
mistakes: Do not say 책임하다 — 책임 is not a verb; use 책임을 지다 instead.
Do not swap 책임 with 의무; 책임 is being answerable for an outcome, while 의무 is a duty you are required to perform.

usage: to have an obligation / to be obligated
the standard pattern; pairs with -아/어야 한다 ideas of must
set phrase with 다하다 to do fully; sounds formal and earnest
N의 의무 names a specific civic duty, common in formal writing
adverb form for things you must do, not by choice
examples: 국민은 세금을 낼 의무가 있어요.
Citizens have a duty to pay taxes.
V-(으)ㄹ 의무가 있다 means an obligation to do something
저는 제 의무를 다했을 뿐이에요.
I only fulfilled my duty.
modest reply when thanked for doing what was required
이 교육은 의무적으로 들어야 해요.
You have to take this training as a requirement.
의무적으로 stresses that it is mandatory, not optional
nuance: 의무 is a duty imposed from outside, by law, rules, or a role, that you are required to carry out, and it is often paired with 권리 (rights) as its natural opposite. It feels more formal and rule-bound than 책임, which is about being answerable for results. You will see 의무 a lot in official and civic contexts like taxes, military service, and school.
mistakes: Do not use 의무 for a casual favor; it implies a binding requirement, not a friendly request.
Do not confuse 의무 with 책임; 의무 is a required duty, while 책임 is accountability for an outcome.

usage: the core pattern; states an entitlement you are owed
주장하다 to claim; used when standing up for what you are owed
기본 + 권리 for fundamental rights, common in social topics
보호하다 to protect; appears in formal and legal contexts
examples: 누구나 자유롭게 말할 권리가 있어요.
Everyone has the right to speak freely.
V-(으)ㄹ 권리가 있다 means the right to do something
소비자는 자신의 권리를 잘 알아야 해요.
Consumers should know their rights well.
common in consumer and social education contexts
권리에는 의무가 따라요.
Obligations follow rights.
권리 and 의무 are frequently paired as opposites
nuance: 권리 is a right in the sense of an entitlement, something you are justly owed and may claim, and it is the natural partner of 의무 (duty). Note that the pronunciation softens to sound like 궐리 because of how the consonants meet. Use 권리 for legal and social entitlements, not for the directional sense of right versus left, which is 오른쪽.
mistakes: Do not confuse 권리 (a right/entitlement) with 오른쪽 (the right side/direction).
Do not say 권리하다 — express it with verbs like 권리를 주장하다 or 권리가 있다.

usage: the most common description; 강하다 strong vs 약하다 weak
used to admit you give in easily, e.g. on a diet
add -력 to emphasize the strength or power of will
to have the will to do something
V-(으)ㄹ 의지가 있다 shows determination to act
examples: 다이어트는 의지가 정말 중요한 것 같아요.
I think willpower is really important for dieting.
natural spoken opinion with -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다
그 사람은 의지가 강해서 끝까지 포기하지 않았어요.
That person has a strong will, so they did not give up to the end.
explaining a result with -아/어서
저는 한국어를 끝까지 배울 의지가 있어요.
I have the will to learn Korean to the end.
expressing personal determination
nuance: 의지 is willpower, the inner determination to push through difficulty, and it is most often described as 강하다 (strong) or 약하다 (weak). It is about resolve and self-control, not a casual wish, so it carries a sense of effort against temptation or hardship. Note this is the homophone meaning will; the verb 의지하다 (to rely on someone) is a separate, related word.
mistakes: Do not confuse the noun 의지 (willpower) with the verb 의지하다 (to lean on / rely on someone).
Do not use 의지 for a light wish like wanting a snack; use it for serious determination.

usage: to be frazzled / too busy to think straight
very common idiom; means overwhelmed, not literally mindless
to pull oneself together / come to one's senses
set phrase; snap back to focus or regain composure
정신적 스트레스 mental stress, as opposed to physical
adverb; doing something so busily you lose track
examples: 요즘 일이 너무 많아서 정신이 없어요.
These days I have so much work that I am frazzled.
the everyday meaning: overwhelmed, not insane
놀라지 말고 정신 차리세요.
Do not panic and pull yourself together.
said to someone who is flustered or in shock
몸도 중요하지만 정신 건강도 챙겨야 해요.
The body matters, but you also have to take care of mental health.
정신 건강 means mental health
nuance: 정신 spans spirit, mind, and mental clarity, and in daily speech it lives mostly in idioms: 정신이 없다 means you are too busy or flustered to focus, and 정신을 차리다 means to regain your composure. It contrasts with 몸 (body) when talking about 정신 건강 (mental health). Treat the idioms as fixed chunks rather than translating word by word.
mistakes: 정신이 없다 does not mean having no mind; it means being frazzled or swamped.
Do not confuse 정신 with 마음; 정신 leans toward mental focus and consciousness, while 마음 is the heart and feelings.

usage: 상상 + 하다 makes the verb; picture something in your mind
to be imaginable / to picture it
상상이 안 되다 means I can't even picture it
add -력 for the faculty of imagination, praised in children
set phrase meaning far more than expected
examples: 그 영화가 얼마나 무서웠는지 상상이 안 돼요.
You can't imagine how scary that movie was.
상상이 안 되다 is the natural way to say unimaginable
어렸을 때 저는 상상력이 풍부한 아이였어요.
When I was young, I was a child with a rich imagination.
상상력이 풍부하다 means to have a vivid imagination
결과가 상상 이상으로 좋았어요.
The result was better than I imagined.
상상 이상으로 stresses exceeding expectations
nuance: 상상 is imagination, the act of forming pictures or scenarios in your mind, and it becomes a verb as 상상하다. The most useful everyday chunk is 상상이 안 되다 (I can't even picture it), used for things too extreme or surprising to grasp. For someone's creative capacity, use 상상력 (imaginative power).
mistakes: Do not confuse 상상 (imagination) with 생각 (thought); 상상 is picturing something unreal or hypothetical.
Avoid 상상이 없다 for I can't imagine it; the idiomatic form is 상상이 안 되다.

usage: 판단 + 하다; to assess a situation and decide
to make a judgment / reach a decision
set phrase with 내리다; sounds deliberate and weighty
add -력 for the ability to judge well
올바른 + 판단 for a right decision, common in advice
examples: 성급하게 판단하지 말고 끝까지 들어 보세요.
Do not judge hastily; listen to the end.
common advice using 판단하다
최종 판단은 본인이 내려야 해요.
You have to make the final judgment yourself.
판단을 내리다 for reaching a decision
힘든 상황에서도 그분은 판단력이 뛰어나요.
Even in tough situations, that person has excellent judgment.
판단력이 뛰어나다 praises good discernment
nuance: 판단 is the act of weighing a situation and forming a conclusion, the mental step of assessing before deciding. It pairs with 내리다 (to hand down) as 판단을 내리다 for arriving at a decision, and 판단력 names the skill of judging well. Use it for reasoned evaluation rather than a snap personal preference.
mistakes: Do not confuse 판단 (assessing and deciding) with 결정 (the final choice itself); 판단 emphasizes the reasoning behind the choice.
Do not say 판단이 하다; the verb is 판단하다 or the phrase 판단을 내리다.

usage: set phrase with 세우다 to set up; how you establish a plan
이루다 to accomplish; reaching what you aimed for
정하다 to fix; settling what you will aim for
to aim for / set as a goal
N을/를 목표로 하다 marks the target you work toward
examples: 올해 목표는 한국어로 자유롭게 대화하는 거예요.
My goal this year is to converse freely in Korean.
common new-year style goal statement
작은 목표부터 하나씩 이루어 나가고 있어요.
I am achieving them one by one, starting from small goals.
목표를 이루다 for accomplishing goals
TOPIK 3급 합격을 목표로 공부하고 있어요.
I am studying with the goal of passing TOPIK level 3.
N을/를 목표로 marks what you aim for
nuance: 목표 is a concrete goal or target you aim at, and it travels with a small family of verbs: 세우다 or 정하다 to set it, and 이루다 or 달성하다 to achieve it. It is more specific and outcome-focused than 꿈 (a dream), which is broader and more emotional. Use 목표 for measurable aims like exams, savings, or fitness.
mistakes: Do not say 목표하다 in writing; prefer 목표를 세우다 or 목표로 하다.
Do not confuse 목표 (a concrete target) with 꿈 (a dream); 목표 is specific and achievable, 꿈 is larger and more aspirational.

usage: 첫 + 인상; the impression you make on first meeting
describes how someone comes across, often about looks or manner
인상(이) 깊다 means it left a deep impression
좋은 인상을 주다 to make a good impression on someone
examples: 그분은 인상이 참 좋아서 금방 친해졌어요.
That person gives such a good impression that we became close quickly.
인상이 좋다 about a warm, likeable manner
면접에서는 첫인상이 정말 중요해요.
First impressions are really important in interviews.
첫인상 in a practical context
그 영화는 결말이 인상 깊었어요.
That movie's ending was very memorable.
인상 깊다 for something that stuck with you
nuance: 인상 is the impression a person or thing leaves on you, how they strike you, and it shows up most in 첫인상 (first impression), 인상이 좋다 (comes across well), and 인상 깊다 (memorable). Be aware this is a homophone: 인상 also means a price hike in 가격 인상, but in the mind/feelings sense it is purely about impressions. Context makes the meaning clear.
mistakes: Do not confuse the feeling 인상 (impression) with the unrelated 인상 meaning a price increase (가격 인상).
인상 깊다 means memorable; do not read it literally as a deep face.

usage: says someone has moral sense; the bare negative 양심이 없다 is a harsh insult
to feel a pang of conscience / guilty
set idiom with 찔리다 to be pricked; you feel bad inside
양심적인 사람 a person who acts on conscience
to keep one's conscience / stay honest
지키다 to keep; to act rightly even when no one watches
examples: 거짓말을 하고 나니까 양심에 찔려요.
After telling a lie, my conscience bothers me.
양심에 찔리다 for a guilty conscience
그분은 양심적으로 일하는 분이에요.
That person works conscientiously.
양심적으로 for acting with integrity
아무도 안 봐도 양심을 지키는 게 중요해요.
Even if no one is watching, keeping your conscience is important.
양심을 지키다 for staying honest
nuance: 양심 is the conscience, your inner sense of right and wrong, and it surfaces in the idiom 양심에 찔리다 (to feel a twinge of guilt) and the adjective 양심적 (conscientious). Saying 양심이 없다 (to have no conscience) is a strong moral criticism, so use it carefully. Pair it with 지키다 to talk about doing the right thing even unobserved.
mistakes: Do not confuse 양심 (moral conscience, right vs wrong) with 의식 (awareness/consciousness).
Be careful with 양심이 없다 — it is a strong insult implying someone is shameless, not a neutral remark.

usage: 기억 + 하다; to hold something in mind
set phrase with 나다; the memory surfaces on its own
the everyday way to say it slipped your mind
to stay in one's memory / be memorable
남다 to remain; something you won't forget
examples: 그분 이름이 갑자기 기억이 안 나요.
I suddenly can't remember that person's name.
기억이 안 나다 is far more natural than 기억하지 않다 here
어릴 때 살던 동네가 아직도 기억에 남아 있어요.
The neighborhood I lived in as a child still stays in my memory.
기억에 남다 for a lasting memory
그날의 좋은 기억을 평생 잊지 못할 거예요.
I will never forget the good memories of that day for my whole life.
기억 as the noun for recollections you treasure
nuance: 기억 is memory or recollection, and the key intermediate skill is using its idioms rather than the bare verb: 기억이 나다 (it comes to mind) and especially 기억이 안 나다 (I can't recall) are how Koreans naturally talk about remembering and forgetting. 기억에 남다 describes something that stays with you. It differs from 추억, which specifically means fond, nostalgic memories of the past.
mistakes: For can't remember, use 기억이 안 나다, not the stiff 기억하지 않다 which sounds like a deliberate choice not to remember.
Do not confuse 기억 (memory/recall in general) with 추억 (fond nostalgic memories).
